utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, General Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Karadzic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. I would like to tender a document that the Prosecutor had on its associated list of exhibits and I overlooked it, but I realise now that it has not been admitted into evidence and it is directly connected to the previous document. So if possible, I would like to tender it now and perhaps we can call it up. That's 65 ter 26 -- 23607, 65 ter 23607. I believe there is a translation, because the document was supposed to be part of a package. And may I put a question in reference to this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, you recall the document that the Prosecutor showed on the 29th of July that had to do with prisoners of war and their guarding just in case so that we would not be cheated.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the last document during the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please take a look at this document. This is a document of the following day sent from the same general. In fact, it is just a recounting of what the general had done. So please take a look. It's the command of the 1st Mountain -- Light Mountain -- Light Infantry Brigade. It says that -- it comes from the security organ, and it says that these people were in the reception centre and that they had been registered.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think it says anything on the face of this document about anybody being registered.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't received an interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is your question, Mr. Karadzic? Do you hear me? Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. I can only hear it now. Yes, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question for the General is to take a look at this document, and if we can leaf through it and scroll down to the end. Could we have page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, do you agree that this also provides a health bulletin, the health status of these prisoners of war, and there is mention that there are several serious -- people in serious condition. And then under (c) it says: "Pursuant to an order and instructions from General Tolimir we have taken all necessary steps within our capabilities. Among other things we have done as follows: We have categorised the prisoners of war. They are housed in three rooms. One room holds the healthy, the other one holds the wounded and injured, and the third holds members of the former leadership. They are receiving medical treatment. They are fed three times a day," and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move on to the next page, the last page. Could we zoom in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please see below. It says: "These Muslims --"

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "The said Muslims complained to General Tolimir and to me too." Oh, yes. I see. It says: "Confiscated the following: 1.800 marks and $25 USA. These men complained to General Tolimir and me, saying that this was done by people commanded by a small black --"

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry, I -- normally I don't interrupt at all, but it looks like we have a technical problem in seeing the English translation because [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was following -- are you not able to follow in your own computer, your e-court?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No. I don't see any display of the English translation at all, and I know it's there somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I hope it will be coming back, but I take it the attorneys should be able to follow the e-court on his own personal computer. Just in case. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just so your Court is aware, my experience is when we try to use that as an expedient, it then essentially logs us off the transcript so we have to log back in repeatedly. So that's one of the problems. Just to let you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now we have it. We have both pages in both versions. General, please see the portion where it says: During -- we have the subtitle "Issues." It was translated as "issues" whereas in Serbian it says "problems that arose." And it says in the area of the elementary school, Tisca-Kladanj road, some money was confiscated, seized from the Muslims who were checked. And then it says above-mentioned Muslims complained to General Tolimir and then in parenthesis "and myself," saying that it was done by men under the command of a short dark-haired man wearing a black beret and with a limp. And then the conclusion evidently refers - and I'll skip the name - some kind of lieutenant who arrived on the scene while the Muslims were still being separated and who then conducted a search in the school and schoolyard. General Tolimir demanded that the case be investigated and that the money be found. Now, sir, is this an exception or, rather, a rule within the Army of Republika Srpska to register prisoners of war, to establish their health condition, and then to accommodate them, the leadership in a different area, to provide food for them and to prevent looting? Is that an exception or a rule?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was the binding rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, could you read -- could you take a look at the bottom of the document where it says: "Authorised by General Tolimir," sent by Captain Zoran Carkic. So although it was sent by a unit in the Podrinje Brigade, I take it that it was sent upon the instruction of General Tolimir. So actual author is General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. I -- it is my view that this intelligence officer from the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade reported orally to General Tolimir on all these issues and that then he ordered him to report to the Main Staff. Now, because he cannot address the Main Staff directly without the -- without the chain of command, then he had to write this down, "Authorised by General Tolimir," and that he's reporting on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. This will be admitted as Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2133, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Now Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, in your testimony on Friday of last week at pages 25210 to 25211, Dr. Karadzic showed you a VRS Main Staff daily operations report to the president for 6 July 1995, and that's D2097. He read you an excerpt from paragraph 6(b) of that have document which said: "The forces have been prepared and grouped for active combat operations towards the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa." And then he asked you: "Do we agree, General, that it's only on the 6th --"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not receiving interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Do you hear me, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you now, but I could not hear the interpreter at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, could you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I will. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the meantime, why don't you upload the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We can, but I actually don't need that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed then.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In your testimony on Friday, Dr. Karadzic showed you a Main Staff daily operations report to the president for 6 July 1995. That's at pages 25210 to 25211. He read you an excerpt from that document which said: "The forces have been prepared and grouped for active --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: "-- combat operations towards the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa." And then he asked you: "Do we agree, General that, it's only on the 6th that the corps decides to respond more actively to these provocations?" And you answered, "Yes."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just as a follow-up from that, I'd like to pull up 65 ter number 15583, please. That's the Operation Krivaja active combat reporter -- pardon me, active combat order from the Drina Corps command signed by General Milenko Zivanovic, dated 2 July 1995. Now --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we're waiting for this document, may I just request that the other document be shown, too, after this one, because "towards Zepa" has a special meaning in our language. It doesn't mean into Zepa but, rather, in that general direction, towards.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we go over to page 2 in the English and page 2 of the B/C/S of this document, paragraph 2, I'd like to draw your attention to a particular passage. You see in paragraph 2 that: "The command of the Drina Corps corps, pursuant to the directive operations number 7 and 7/1, of the VRS Main Staff and on the basis of the situation in the corps zone of responsibility, has the task of carrying out offensive operations with free forces deep in the Drina Corps to divide the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa as soon as possible and reduce them to their urban areas." And under paragraph 4 of the same page, the objective of the operation is set out by: "... a surprise attack to divide and reduce in size the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, improve the tactical position of the forces in the depth of the zone and create conditions for the elimination of the enclaves." So, General, it's clear from this document, isn't it, that the order for the attack on Srebrenica was completed by the 2nd of July and not on the 6th of July as Dr. Karadzic suggested to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please reformulate your question, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, from this document can you see when the order for the attack on Srebrenica was completed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I believe there is a difference in interpreting this. Within the context of reporting, I believe that Defence -- that the Defence asked me whether it was in the reports that it was -- that this date appeared for the first time on the 6th of July, but the task -- the fact itself when I tried to explain the way that directives were drafted, there was also mention of the conclusions and tasks issued by the Drina Corps in the month of January, toward the end of January, and one of their proposals and tasks was the resolution of the issue of enclaves. In other words, there is no -- nothing that is in any way problematic here, because the reporting was -- it started on the 2nd of July, but in the report it says that this was implemented on the 6th of July, as it was stated there, within the context of reporting.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have this document as a Prosecution exhibit, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. This will be admitted as next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4481, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To move on two days further in time, also last Friday at pages 25215 to 25216, Dr. Karadzic showed you another operations report from the Main Staff to the president, dated 8 July 1995, D2099, and he read you the last sentence of paragraph 6(a), which said: "On the part of the front towards Srebrenica, the --" and I'll spell it because I don't think I can give justice to its pronunciation, T --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we just upload the document. It's easier to follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. D2099. Paragraph 6(a).

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: On the part of the -- paragraph 6(a) reads: "On the part of the front towards Srebrenica, the Tri Sise features were seized by us." And the seizure of those features were also mentioned in 6(b). He also asked whether those were three hills and you said that they were there elevations. And my first question to you is, General: What does the word Sise mean in your language?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are geographic forms that look like a breast, a female breast, three tits, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you know what the strategic significance of the seizure of those features was to the VRS at that time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were probably dominant features. I don't know. I can't tell you as I sit here. I don't have the map here before me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, maybe we could look at 65 ter 23466. It's a very urgent Drina Corps forward command post report to the VRS Main Staff from General Krstic on this same date, 8 July 1995. Paragraph 2 of this document says: "In a powerful assault on the axis of Zeleni Jadar-Zivkovo Brdo-Srebrenica, our forces seized control over the key installations on this axis (Biljeg, Visovi, Tri Sise, the village of Ljubisavci) and created favourable conditions for an incursion into Srebrenica." So, General, when you replied to Dr. Karadzic, were you aware of the significance of the seizure of these elevations vis-a-vis the take-over of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is the basis of your objection.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the basis is this: This report only says that the conditions were created. I doesn't say that that was the intent. The question is leading in the sense that it assumes that the decision had already been made, whereas it was only on the 9th, in the evening, that I was informed that the conditions had been now created for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, I don't think the question is leading. The question was simply whether he aware of this. Yes. Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Would you like me to repeat the question, General, or are you able to answer it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard your question. I was not aware of the strategic position of these three -- Tri Sise vis-a-vis the protected area, but the issue arises whether this feature was within the protected areas itself or not. I really don't know. And you asked me whether I knew then and I didn't. I didn't know what the position of Tri Sise vis-a-vis the protected area.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have this document as a Prosecution exhibit, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P4482, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now just on the subject of protected areas in respect of that Main Staff report, D2099, we just looked at, you recall that Dr. Karadzic asked you about the -- the area he said is: "... Zeleni Jadar to the south of Srebrenica between Srebrenica and Zepa which was supposed to have been in our territory. It was not a protected area." And your reply was that: "In physical terms it's located between the enclaves." So did you know, General, before you gave that answer that Zeleni Jadar was the location of a manned United Nations observation post?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't really have that recollection. I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So did you know then that that post was attacked and captured by VRS forces using heavy weapons on 8 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you know that seven UNPROFOR soldiers from Zeleni Jadar OP surrendered to the VRS and were taken into VRS custody and transferred to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to make an observation here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness wasn't there at the time and the president was reported that they had fled over to our side. All these questions have to do with what the president knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, she asked the question and he can answer as far as he knows. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Would you like me to repeat the question about the seven UNPROFOR --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think I'm going to repeat --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are hearing French translation. Could you repeat.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Would you like me to repeat the question, General, or do you remember it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you know that seven UNPROFOR soldiers from Zeleni Jadar were arrested and taken into VRS custody and transferred to Bratunac on the 8th of July?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I did not know, but I think that that is not what the report said, I mean, the part of the report that was quoted.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just one more question about this situation. Did you know that UNPROFOR filed a protest with the VRS Main Staff about this operation?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not come across this protest.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. To move on to another subject, on the subject of convoys Dr. Karadzic, at pages 25270 to 25271, showed you a copy of a document from Momir Nikolic dated 10 December 1994, admitted as D2122, relating to the movement of an MSF convoy into Srebrenica which was found to contain plumbing materials and tools which hadn't been approved by the co-ordinating body for humanitarian aid and was confiscated. And referring to this document, Dr. Karadzic asked: "Do you agree that this is yet further proof of abuse in and by the enclaves?" And you answered: "Yes." And then when asked why this document hadn't been shown to its author when he came here to testify at the Tribunal, Dr. Karadzic said: "We're going to show that potato chips and several other things were used for smuggling ammunition and used for firing at our people." So I'd like to know before you answered Dr. Karadzic, did you actually see that the document he showed from you Mr. Nikolic had nothing whatsoever to do with allegations of ammunition smuggling?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to see the document again, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So now whether you can answer the question whether this is related to ammunition smuggling, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It relates to other goods that are not in the function of this organisation PMF. However, with appropriate tools, it is possible to smuggle war supplies well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Maybe what I could do, General, is show you something that Mr. Nikolic, the author of this document, actually did say about allegations of weapon smuggling into Srebrenica, and that's 65 ter 16750, a record of an interview that Mr. Nikolic had with the Dutch Institute for War Documentation, or NIOD, on 20 October 2000. And this is a document that Mr. Karadzic actually did invoke with Mr. Nikolic when he appeared here.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And when the document is up in both languages, perhaps we could go to paragraph 24. In English that's on page 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, General, paragraph 24 says: "The VRS Supreme Command --"

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, we have two versions of English paragraph 24. Just one second. Paragraph 24 reads: "The VRS Supreme Command sent requests to halt convoys on the Yellow Bridge. N," referring to Nikolic, "stated with great certainty that he had never found any weapons on the convoys. Whoever claims that is lying. We should send everyone who makes such claims to Nikolic. If anyone was supposed to know this, it was Nikolic." Would you like to comment, General?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't want to go into Nikolic's statements. However, on the basis of all the reports that we received from our subordinates and from these check-points, their reports were different.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, General, do you, on sick leave from January to July 1995, during which period you were not on active duty, claim to know better than the VRS security officer whose job it was to check convoys actually going into the enclave?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I'm going to object to that question as being argumentative and also quite unfair to the witness given that the Prosecutor brought lots of documents to that period according to which it wanted -- when it wanted to have an answer favourable to its case from this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let us proceed. You can move on, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to go on -- or stay roughly with the same topic, actually, and that has to do with levels of food in the enclave. Dr. Karadzic showed you a number of convoy-related documents in the fall of 1993 and 1995. And he said to you at page 25261, General: "If I told you that there were witnesses here who testified that for months on end convoys didn't arrive, would you tell them that they did not say -- state the truth, to say the least?" And your answer was: "Well, I wouldn't need to say anything. It's all here." So I'd like to show you a United Nations report on what the actual food situation was like for the people in the Srebrenica enclave.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So in that regard, could we see P04142. It's a United Nations military observer report, dated 8 July 1995, on the food situation in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, General, paragraph 1 of this document, line -- or subparagraph (a) or line (a), lists the total population of Srebrenica at 42.000, 85 per cent of whom are refugees or displaced persons. And then 2(a) reports that the foot stock in the UNHCR warehouse is almost zero. 3(a) says that the UNHCR planned convoy, the planned convoy, for a week is three. However, due to the persistent refusal by the Bosnian Serb Army to allow into these enclaves an average of one arrives per week. And then it remarks: "Even if the UNHCR planned convoys were implemented, this would have served barely about 65 per cent of the needs of the ... population. However, with the present rate of delivery, less than 25 per cent of the needs is being met."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just a second. Are we looking at the same document? The B/C/S translation is correct translation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not all of it. There's a reference here to prices of particular goods.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In B/C/S we need to go over to paragraph 3, which is on the second page, and I think the confusion might have arisen from some odd numbering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Why do you have it different numbering? Shall we take a look at next page. Yes. I think we -- this is it. Yes. Please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, so here's the situation also in black and white of what it was like inside the enclaves in July of 1995. So I'm wondering whether this affects your answer, the answer you gave to Dr. Karadzic, in any way.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer given to Dr. Karadzic had to do with a series of documents and weekly convoys with humanitarian aid for Srebrenica and the other enclaves, Zepa, Gorazde. So I don't see anything controversial there. That series of weekly reports showed the period after directive 7. That period of time was involved in that series of documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, do you remember the date of this document that I read to you, and we could go back over to page 1, dates from July 8th, 1995? That's also the period after the issuance of directive 7, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we actually have a look at directive 7? It's P838. Excuse me, could we go over to page 14 in English and the top of page 21 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this is under the heading -- the passage I want you to look at is under the heading "Support for combat operations." Paragraph 6.1 which deals with moral and psychological support says, and you see it on the page in front of you, General: "The relevant state and military organs responsible for work with UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations shall, through the planned and unobtrusively restrictive issuing of permits, reduce and limit the logistics support of UNPROFOR to the enclaves and the supply of material resources --"

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not on this part of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It is, actually. If we could pull the B/C/S page down a little bit so the General can see the top paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had only the heading, "Moral and psychological support," and now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: "... the supply of material resources to the Muslim population making them dependent on our goodwill, while at the same time avoiding condemnation by the international community and international public opinion." It's -- General, is it clear from this document and the evidence you've seen that this is exactly the policy being followed with respect to convoy movement to the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly whether it reflects policy, but this text that was written by the sector or someone from the sector for moral guidance, religious and legal affairs could be interpreted in that way. But since directive number 7 was implemented to a tiny per cent, I don't know whether this paragraph reflects the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again I have an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The General has already answered. Let's continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to move over to events on 16 July 1995, which were dealt with at pages 25232 to 25235 of Friday's transcript, and in relation to that, Dr. Karadzic showed you, General, another VRS Main Staff operations report to him on that date, admitted as D2101. And he read to you, again from paragraph number 6, mention of a corridor for the pull-out of the civilian population which was used by about 7.000 mainly unarmed civilians --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, it's always easy to follow with the document. Why don't we upload it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course. D2101. Apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Halfway through the paragraph 6(a) at the bottom of the page in B/C/S, at the top of the page in English, you see mention of a corridor which was used by about 7.000 mainly unarmed civilians, men, women, and children. And in respect of this paragraph, Doctor asked you: "Do we agree that this is the first part of the 16th of July, informing me that within that column that was breaking through there were civilians as well, that these civilians, except perhaps in the first report, were not mentioned as part of the column," and you agreed. And then he said: "So this could also pacify my advisors that they had gotten through so that they could not alarm me. They had gotten through." And your response was: "Since they had gotten through, there was nothing special, nothing specially dramatic, that is." And I'm just wondering, do you actually know, General, the full extent of the information that Dr. Karadzic actually received about this information?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what extent you are referring to. The extent is provided in this report. I don't know whether he had other information.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Maybe we could turn to 65 ter number 32210A, which is an intercept dated 16 July 1995, at 1529, with someone from the Main Staff and the duty officer at a location code-named Palma, which the Prosecution will be calling evidence is the code-name for the Zvornik Brigade. And this, General, is an example of the other information Dr. Karadzic had.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. How could I have had that information available?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It hasn't been released, I was told, Ms. Edgerton. Yes. That was the question I take it Ms. Edgerton was going to ask to the General.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's going to be released in moments, and apologies for that, Your Honours. 31120A. I've done it again with numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Maybe -- this is a handwritten B/C/S transcript. If the General could have a look and in the event he doesn't find it legible, we have a typewritten B/C/S transcript as well that we could offer. So, General, the interlocutor in this conversation from the Main Staff explains he has to get permission from the main boss and says: "Well, that's why I'm calling you from the main head of state --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have the typewritten version? Why don't we upload it for the benefit of the General.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 31120C should be the B/C/S typewritten report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. In the meantime, we -- yes. Yes. Let us continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it just be zoomed in a bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So the interlocutor from the Main Staff says: "That's why I'm calling you from the main head of state," and explains that they got a call from someone by the name of Stanisavljevic from Novi Karakaj, and he advises the Palma duty officer to have Vinko tell him what happened and send it right away. And then later he says to dictate what's been done and send it urgently, right away, to the Main Staff, the conditions and the rest, to the Main Staff as soon as possible. General, who is the main head of state in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of Republika Srpska? Dr. Radovan Karadzic. If Republika Srpska is what is meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Indeed that's what I meant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have a look at also D02002, which is an intercept of another conversation about half an hour later, 4.15 that same date, between the Main Staff duty officer and General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it be zoomed in.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So here, General, the duty officer says: "Well, it's like this, sir. I've just sent a telegram to Toso. Well, the President called a short while ago and said that he had been informed by Karisik that Pandurevic has arranged passage for the Muslims ... to that territory." General, who was Toso?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume it was General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And who is Karisik?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A person with the last name of Karisik was in the police, if it has to do with that person.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you know what his duties were in the police?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, General, is it clear from these two intercepted conversations that Dr. Karadzic was briefed by his advisors on the situation on that day and personally intervened with the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, when -- I used to tell Mr. Karadzic it's a leading question when it begins with "is it clear." Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, based on what you've seen in these last two documents, are you prepared to comment on the level of information Dr. Karadzic had available to him as regards this situation?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on these documents, you can see that the participants in the conversation are intermediaries of a kind. Whether this was done in a timely fashion, detailed fashion, whether the information was accurately conveyed I can't say, but this shows that the head of state is referred to and there are third parties who are communicating with each other. As to whether they're able of conveying this at the same time or whether they will wait for a certain period of time, well, I don't know. I don't know these participants in the conversation. So I don't know how rapidly this can reach the president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When was it that you returned to the Main Staff, General Obradovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 17th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: After you returned, did you not hear about this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that I subsequently heard about that decision taken by the Zvornik Brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I have the first intercept, 32210C, as a Prosecution exhibit, please. The second one is already exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark the -- yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I don't believe the witness confirmed anything about that document. I don't see how it can be marked for identification through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's very relevant to the question put to the witness with respect to the D document, D2101, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's relevant but the witness didn't have anything to say about it, so I don't see how it can be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now witness said it was arranged by Zvornik Brigade, did he not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness said that he learned afterwards that the column -- allowing the column to go through was arranged by the Zvornik Brigade, but I don't see how that relates to the admissibility of that intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Ms. Edgerton, would you like to respond?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I do with your indulgence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: First of all, just with respect to the threshold that I spoke with Your Honours about on Friday, I wouldn't like to see the threshold to be a moving one, and documents that Dr. Karadzic have -- has tendered or offered to the witness have been admitted on the simple basis of the witness acknowledging that what he reads in the document is what he reads in the document. That's the first thing. Not only did he confirm aspects of this intercept, he confirmed in the first one that the president was the head of state, that it's -- the obvious connection to the column referred to in the -- in the report to the president, Your Honour, is -- is linkage enough, I would suggest, in terms of relevance to -- for Your Honours to find that we've passed that threshold in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If I could just be heard briefly in reply. The Prosecution wants to use this intercept to show a certain level of knowledge by Dr. Karadzic. That's a very strongly contested issue in the case. So not only is the intercept quite removed from Dr. Karadzic, second- or third- or fourth-hand or whatever, but this witness hasn't been able to speak to that issue at all. So if they want to introduce the intercept, it ought to be through somebody who had some knowledge so that they could be cross-examined and that so we could advance the Chamber's level of knowledge about that issue, but this witness doesn't advance that knowledge at all and exhibit shouldn't be admitted through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we see that intercept again. Can you upload it so that I can see the passage. The only question you put to the witness was -- was who was the main head of state. But let us see how it was ... 31120A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, can you assist us with this aspect of the evidence: Based on these documents, you concede the participants are intermediaries of a kind. This shows that the head of state is referred to and third parties are communicating with each other. That wouldn't have any bearing at all, would you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I think it does have bearing. First of all, I don't think it can be said that the speaker -- any of these speakers are the intermediary of Dr. Karadzic as the head of state. This is somebody speaking from the Main Staff of the army to the Drina Corps. So if there's somebody purporting to speak for the head of state, I don't think it can be quite linked that closely to Dr. Karadzic. And I think that is another reason for why the document should not be admitted, because it's too removed to be attributed to Dr. Karadzic. Anybody can be invoking his name or his position if they want to convince somebody to do something. So I don't think that this is clear. It's a level of hearsay that we don't know how many times removed, and to that extent, I think it's relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, may we hear you in reply to that particular point.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, first of all, there is no question of remoteness of any of the speakers or intermediaries. One of them is General Mladic. One of them is General Tolimir. So I think those can be linked quite closely to Dr. Karadzic. It's -- it's not removed at all, and just further, in fact, Your Honours, the witness himself has -- if I can have your indulgence for a moment. No. Dr. Karadzic himself has raised the issue of the level of knowledge that he received in his cross-examination of this witness from members of the VRS Main Staff, and this clearly shows that he is not only receiving a greater level of knowledge than he suggested, but his intermediaries in this case are members of the VRS Main Staff. He has directly contacted the VRS Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, I didn't follow when you said that one of them is General Mladic and one -- the other is Tolimir. What did you mean, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The second conversation that's no longer on the screen in front of us, Your Honour, involves General Mladic speaking with an intermediary from the VRS Main Staff. General Mladic is not heard, but the interlocutor has been identified as General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are not referring to this specific intercept.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No. This was the first one, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And sorry, I misspoke, Your Honour, when I noted that one of the interlocutors is General Tolimir. General Tolimir was referred to in the intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where? Not this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, no. He was referred to in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In D2002, in CSB report.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not here.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, not in this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The issues raised in this intercept is -- without doubt has reason from the lines of questioning Mr. Karadzic's cross-examination. In that respect, it is relevant and the issues of weight is something to be assessed by the Chamber later on, and the authenticity will be dealt with at a later stage together with all the other intercepts. On that basis we mark it for identification as next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI P4483, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'd just like to move on to one final area and that has to do with orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: At page 25194 of the transcript, Dr. Karadzic put to you a question to the effect that -- whether you agreed that the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a collective presidential body retained only the strategic level of command within its remit. It was a document-based question, and you said, yes, that's the conclusion of this provision. And then following that, you explained to the Chamber the difference between strategic, operational, and command -- and tactical command levels, saying that the corps were at the operational level. They make operational decisions. Whereas brigades and lower ranking units are at the tactical level. The strategic level is at the state level. I wonder in that regard if you have any actual knowledge of tactical orders issued by Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to play you one example, please, and it's a recording, a conversation excerpted from a Dictaphone tape seized from the Mladic residence, and the Prosecution believes and will be adducing evidence through other witnesses that the conversation occurred sometime on the afternoon of 8 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, did you recognise the voices of either of the interlocutors to this conversation?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certain about Dr. Karadzic but not about Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes that the witness is barely audible. Could the witness please approach the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you speak into the microphone, General Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I could recognise Dr. Karadzic's voice, but the voice of Zivanovic is not as clear. I didn't speak to him so much. I didn't have the opportunity to listen to him that often, but I think it was his voice.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When you say Zivanovic, who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Drina Corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: At a certain point in this conversation, Dr. Karadzic asks General Zivanovic: "Are the tits ours?" And he responds: "They are. They are. They are for the first time." And Dr. Karadzic then says again: "That's good. Let's not give up on the tits no matter what." Now, General, given your explanation of what that word means in your language and the documents that we've looked at earlier today that describe a feature called "tits" that was taken over by VRS forces on 8 July 1995, do you have any idea what Dr. Karadzic might be referring to in this conversation when he uses that same word?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that he was referring to a geographical feature.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in this conversation, Dr. Karadzic tells Zivanovic that he can probably get reinforcements for him and discusses the deployment of the Zvornik MUP on the Trnovo front. So back to orders. Is organising the deployment of reinforcements from one front to the other answer an exercise of strategic, operational, or tactical-level command?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On what basis, Mr. Karadzic? In the meantime -- just a second. Ms. Edgerton, do you have the 65 ter number for this?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 35043A. Apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here there is a confusion being created. The army can't mobilise the MUP. The president has to do that. So the witness has to be shown that this concerns the MUP forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it's not a proper objection on your part. Yes, General, can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this isn't a case of issuing an order. This is the result of certain requests from the corps command concerning the engagement of certain forces. The Ministry of the Interior has responsibility for MUP units, and the supreme commander takes decisions that concern them. So the minister probably told the president about a request to engage the MUP in a certain stretch of territory, and he said that they had been engaged in Treskavica or somewhere. So the army does not have responsibility for commanding MUP units. They can be subordinated to them and -- at some point, but with the authorisation of the president, but the request has to go through the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. 65 ter number again, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I wonder, General, if you could actually answer the question, because the question was: Is organising the deployment of reinforcements from one front to the other an exercise of strategic, operational, or tactical-level command?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, once again, it's not a matter of deciding at such a low level. It is a matter of a reaction to the requests from lower levels, requests to engage MUP units. The location of engagement for those MUP units depend on the corps command decisions, if he receives authorisation for such units, because he requests such units for the purpose of certain needs since he does not have sufficient forces at his disposal.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Also in this conversation, Dr. Karadzic asks that instructions for journalists be prepared for him to sign off on. So is Dr. Karadzic's personal involvement in the propaganda aspect of an operation an exercise of strategic, operational, or tactical-level command?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't place that in the category of command. He probably didn't have a spokesperson. For example, NATO pact has Jamie Shea who deals with such matters so that commanders don't have to appear directly before the public.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Who is the Krstic and Krle referred to in this conversation?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that it concerns General Radislav Krstic. I assume they called him Krle. He was the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps. And around the 20th, there was a rotation and he was appointed as commander of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So in this conversation we heard Dr. Karadzic order Krstic to go "full steam ahead." Now, is an order like this from the supreme commander in the middle of an ongoing operation an exercise of strategic, operational, or tactical-level command?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you see that this is an order? It's a conversation. The question implies or suggests the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton is asking the question to the witness. Yes. Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I've asked the question. Would we like it to be repeated?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not necessary. I didn't notice such an imperative in the conversation, but in one intercepted conversation when General Mladic spoke to Krle, he said in an imperative manner: "Move ahead." But I didn't hear such an imperative tone here. In this case, it seems to be more a case of encouragement, "Move ahead."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We're not hearing any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The accused said the question can change the meaning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. Witness has answered the question. Please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I actually have nothing further in redirect, Your Honour, but I need to correct myself in one regard. When I introduced this conversation, I said it's our belief that it took place on the 8th of July -- pardon me, Your Honours. I need to -- my colleagues are trying to get my attention.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now having heard from my colleagues, Your Honour, I'd like to ask this: I would like to go into one further area very briefly, if we could, after the break. I just note what time it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a moment. Have we have not admitted or marked for identification that refers to "full stream ahead," which is a separate intercept?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Not yet, and I wonder if we could do that before the break, Your Honour. But, Your Honour, I'm wondering if this might be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And date is correct, 8th -- on or about the 8th of July?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I will check that, because I was receiving notes during the examination-in-chief, so I'll also check that over the break. But if I might make one submission with regard to the intercept, Your Honour. Given that we've had the audio, we've played the audio, the witness has recognised Dr. Karadzic as one of the interlocutors, I wonder if this might exceptionally be admitted rather than marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I hear from you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. My first thought is I was wondering why this wasn't introduced when Mr. Blaszczyk came and testified to the contents of the Mladic searches. That would have been the logical place to lay a foundation for this exhibit. Having heard from this witness, all he can do is identify a voice, which is relevant, but I don't think he's been able to comment on the substance of the exhibit. So we object on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Apart from tendering this document, how long would you need to complete your re-examination, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I hope about five minutes, Your Honours, but I would need some time during the break to speak to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I was wondering whether you could continue because we need another break before the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I recognise that, Your Honours, and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But we will take a break now for half an hour and resume at five past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, last year on 4th of February in the decision of judicial notice decision, we ruled as follows: "Therefore, declaration from persons who are neither participants in the conversation themselves nor intercept operators are not sufficient for the purpose of establishing an intercept's authenticity. The Chamber is thus not satisfied that the authenticity of the following intercept was sufficiently established." I think this case should be no different. In order for you to tender that intercept, it should have been discussed through Mr. Blaszczyk, who at least could have provided at least some foundation as to how this intercept came into the possession of the Prosecution. Probably you can find a way of having this intercept admitted after at least some foundation has been laid later on. So we will not admit this intercept with this witness. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can it then be marked for identification, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll mark it for identification as next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit MFI P4484, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to come back to the date, Your Honours, I had expressed some doubt in my articulation of that date of that document on the record, and I've looked into it and I was absolutely correct. It is on or about the 8th of July, 1995. Just so that's not unclear. And I have following the break, as I had indicated, one final question for the General.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, in answering -- in identifying who Krle and Krstic was in the intercept that we discussed prior to the break, you indicated that it concerned Radislav Krstic. You assumed they called them Krle, and you indicated he was the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps, and around the 20th, there was a rotation and he was appointed as commander of the Drina Corps. utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd now like to read out a summary of Mr. Erdemovic's testimony in the Popovic case. Drazen Erdemovic joined the VRS in April 1994 and was assigned to a special unit. In October 1994, that unit was named the 10th Sabotage Detachment. In 1995, the detachment had 50 to 60 members divided into two platoons located in Bijeljina and Vlasenica. The witness was a member of the Bijeljina platoon. The commander of the detachment was 2nd Lieutenant Milorad Pelemis, and the detachment was supervised at the VRS Main Staff level by Colonel Petar Salapura from the intelligence centre. On the afternoon of 10 July 1995, the witness and 30 to 40 other members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment arrived in the Srebrenica area and spent the night at an elevation above the town. The next day, together with 15 soldiers from another VRS unit known as the Drina Wolves, they entered the town of Srebrenica itself. Before they entered the town, 2nd Lieutenant Pelemis ordered the unit not to shoot at civilians. However, when they reached the centre of the town, an able-bodied Muslim man surrendered to them, and although the man said that he was not a member of the army, Pelemis ordered a soldier named Zoran, nickname Maljic, from the Vlasenica platoon, to kill this man. Mr. Erdemovic saw Maljic slit the throat of this Muslim man. The detachment spent the night in Srebrenica and returned to Vlasenica the next day. When they arrived, they heard that a UN transporter driven by Lieutenant Pelemis had overturned and killed a member of the 10th Sabotage Detachment named Dragan Koljivrat. On 13 July, Mr. Erdemovic and others left for Koljivrat's funeral in Trebinje. They returned to Vlasenica on the morning of 15 July. On the morning of 16 July 1995, another member of the 10th Sabotage Detachment named Brano Gojkovic came to Mr. Erdemovic and said that he and two other members should get their weapons ready and prepare to go on an assignment. In total, eight members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment set off from Vlasenica that day: Drazen Erdemovic, Marko Boskic, Franc Kos, Vlastimir Golijan, Brano Gojkovic, Aleksandar Cvetkovic, Zoran Goronja, and Stanko Savanovic. Brano Gojkovic was in charge of this group. They stopped at some military barracks in Zvornik and Brano Gojkovic and Aleksandar Cvetkovic went inside. Shortly afterwards, they came back out with a tall, corpulent lieutenant-colonel with a greyish hair in a VRS uniform and two Drina Corps military policemen. The Lieutenant-Colonel and two MPs got into an olive green Opel Kadett car, and the eight members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment then followed the Lieutenant-Colonel and the two MPs in the Opel Kadett to the Branjevo Farm in Pilica. At the farm, the Lieutenant-Colonel went into a side office and everyone who was in that office, apart from one man, came out and left the farm. The Lieutenant-Colonel then came back out and spoke with Brano Gojkovic, and Gojkovic then instructed Erdemovic's group that buses carrying civilians from Srebrenica would be arriving and that these civilians were to be killed. The Lieutenant-Colonel and the two MPs left shortly after the first bus arrived. The first group of 10 civilians who were taken off the bus were blindfolded and had their hands tied behind their backs. They were escorted to a site about 1- to 200 metres away from the bus and lined up in a row with their backs to the execution squad. Once they were in position, Brano Gojkovic gave the order to shoot, and Mr. Erdemovic and the seven other members of the 10 Sabotage Detachment opened fire on the civilians with automatic rifles. A second group of civilians followed, and the executions were carried out like this, in groups of ten, from around 10.00 a.m. to 3.00 or 4.00 p.m. Mr. Erdemovic estimated that approximately 1.000 to 1.200 civilians were executed at the Branjevo Farm that day. At one point during the executions, Aleksandar Cvetkovic suggested that they use an M-84 machine-gun because it was faster than using automatic rifles. However, a quarrel soon broke out over the use of the machine-gun because it was causing severe injuries to the civilians without actually killing them. Early in the afternoon, a unit of eight to ten soldiers from Bratunac arrived and joined in the executions. These soldiers from Bratunac kicked, punched, and cursed at the prisoners. They also beat some prisoners with rifle butts and metal bars that they found on the farm. At around 3.00 or 4.00, the Lieutenant-Colonel returned as the last bus of prisoners were being executed. The Lieutenant-Colonel said that there were some 500 prisoners at the Pilica cultural centre who also needed to be executed, but Mr. Erdemovic and some other members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment refused this order. Instead, the unit from Bratunac went with the Lieutenant-Colonel and participated in these executions. The witness and the other members of the detachment were instructed to meet the Lieutenant-Colonel in a coffee bar in Pilica just across the road from the Pilica cultural centre. When they arrived, Mr. Erdemovic saw several dead bodies in front of the cultural hall and heard gunfire and explosions coming from that direction. He also saw a civilian check-point outside the cultural centre manned by two or three RS MUP members in blue camouflage uniforms. Mr. Erdemovic sat in the coffee bar while Brano Gojkovic and others sat separately with the Lieutenant-Colonel. After a while one of the soldiers from Bratunac came into the coffee bar and reported that everything was finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Erdemovic, I have some additional questions on a number of areas. To start off with, I'd like to go back to 1994 and ask you a couple of questions about the unit that you joined and that then became the 10th Sabotage Detachment in October 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If I can have 65 ter number 23624 in e-court. Mr. President, this is a document that we moved to add to our 65 ter list in connection with the testimony of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any objection, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That's granted, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Erdemovic, do you recall being shown this document yesterday?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
